974.title: Napoleon's Sanhedrin (1807)
974.hook: Napoleon questions Jewish leaders about loyalty and law
974.howItsDone: The Talmudic principle dina de-malkhuta dina is still taught in Jewish law today, as the basis for keeping a country's civil laws, such as paying taxes, alongside the commandments.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a vote in Paris made Jews citizens, as individuals. Your line was a door opened, with a price. Which right did you use on purpose? Today, an emperor wants to know what those citizens really think. Day nine hundred seventy-four.

A list of questions lands on the table of a gathering of Jewish leaders in Paris. It comes from the emperor himself, Napoleon. They are not questions about theology. They are sharper than that. Does your law allow a man more than one wife? Is a Jewish divorce valid without the state's courts? May a Jew marry a Christian? Do you consider the French your brothers? Is France your country, and will you defend it? Everyone in the room understands the question underneath all the questions: can you be fully Jewish and fully French at the same time? Today, Napoleon's Sanhedrin.
screen: `A LIST FROM THE EMPEROR.` → `WIVES, DIVORCE, MARRIAGE, BROTHERS.` → `CAN YOU BE BOTH?`

segments.voice: Napoleon first called together an assembly of Jewish notables, rabbis and lay leaders, to answer his questions. Then, to give their answers religious weight, he did something theatrical. He summoned a Grand Sanhedrin, borrowing the name of the ancient high court of Jewish law in Jerusalem, a court of the distant past. So how did they answer? Carefully, and within Jewish law. A man may have only one wife; they pointed to the old ban on taking more. A religious divorce should follow a civil one. France is our country and we will defend it; the French are our brothers. On marrying Christians they walked a narrow line, saying such marriages were valid in civil law while rabbis would not perform them. And underneath many answers lay one principle from the Talmud, a saying of the sage Shmuel, in Aramaic: dina de-malkhuta dina, the law of the kingdom is the law. In matters like taxes, property and civil order, Jewish law itself tells Jews to keep the law of the land they live in. That principle was not invented for Napoleon. It was already there, in the Talmud. What the Sanhedrin did was draw a line with it. Here, in civil life, the state's law binds us. There, in the commandments between a person and God, our Torah does. The emperor wanted loyalty. The assembly gave it, and kept something back that was not theirs to give. That is what a loyal question can do: make you say clearly where your loyalties lie, and where they stop.
screen: `AN ASSEMBLY, THEN A GRAND SANHEDRIN.` · `CAREFUL ANSWERS WITHIN JEWISH LAW.` · `DINA DE-MALKHUTA DINA.` · then, large: `WHERE LOYALTY LIES, AND WHERE IT STOPS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: answer one question honestly. Settle into your seat and let your breath slow. Think of a question someone has asked you, or that you've been avoiding asking yourself, about where your loyalties lie. To a job, a family, a friend, a community, a belief. Don't answer it fast. Let it sit. Then try to answer it the way the Sanhedrin did: carefully, without flattering anyone, saying clearly what you will give, and what you will keep. You don't have to say it out loud. Just let the answer be true. The bell holds the time.
Napoleon's Sanhedrin. The Jewish assembly the emperor summoned to answer his questions about loyalty and law, and the Grand Sanhedrin that confirmed its answers. Today's word.
Your line: loyal questions. Today, when someone asks where you stand, answer plainly, and notice where your yes ends. Day nine hundred seventy-four.

975.title: Reform begins
975.hook: German Jews change services: sermons, organs, the vernacular
975.howItsDone: Reform synagogues today commonly hold services that mix Hebrew with the local language and include instrumental music, while Orthodox synagogues keep a traditional Hebrew service without instruments on Shabbat.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Napoleon's Sanhedrin: the law of the kingdom is the law, and a careful line drawn with it. Your line was loyal questions. Where did your yes end? Today, Jews in Germany ask a different question, about their own synagogues. Day nine hundred seventy-five.

A Sabbath morning in a German town. The Jewish families walk in to pray, and the room sounds different. There is an organ. A choir sings. Some of the prayers are in German, the language these families now speak at home and at work. And then a man stands up and gives a sermon, in German, polished and earnest. Some in the room are moved to tears; for once they understand every word. Others walk out shaken; to them this is no longer the synagogue of their parents. Today, Reform begins.
screen: `AN ORGAN, A CHOIR.` → `PRAYERS IN GERMAN.` → `TEARS, AND PEOPLE WALKING OUT.`

segments.voice: The new citizens of yesterday's story faced a real worry. Their children were learning German, going to German schools, entering German professions. And some of them were drifting away from Judaism altogether, finding the synagogue long, hard to follow, and out of step with the life they lived the rest of the week. A group of German Jews decided the answer was to change the service itself. A layman named Israel Jacobson built a house of prayer with an organ and held services with German hymns and German sermons. In Hamburg, a congregation opened a temple with its own new prayer book, shorter, partly in German, and with changes to some prayers about the return to Zion. They wanted worship that was dignified, understandable, and modern. The organ became a symbol of the whole fight. Supporters could point to the Psalms. Here is a line of Psalm one hundred fifty, as the King James Bible renders it: "Praise him with stringed instruments and organs." Opponents answered that playing an instrument on the Sabbath breaks the Sabbath, that the organ imitated the church, and that the prayers were not anyone's to rewrite. Traditional rabbis published rulings against the Hamburg prayer book. The reformers feared losing the young to the world. The traditionalists feared losing the prayers their parents had said, word for word. The Reform movement grew out of these first changes, and so did new ways of defending tradition, which we'll meet tomorrow. And the question the organ raised, what may change in a service and who gets to decide, would be argued in synagogue after synagogue.
screen: `CHILDREN DRIFTING AWAY.` · `ORGAN, CHOIR, GERMAN SERMONS.` · `PRAISE HIM WITH ORGANS?` · then, large: `TWO FEARS, ONE SYNAGOGUE.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: notice one change you've lived through. Sit comfortably and breathe out slowly. Think of something that changed around you: a family tradition done a new way, a community that modernized, a job that went digital, a holiday that looks different now than when you were small. Let yourself feel both sides. What was gained? What was lost? Who welcomed it, and who walked out quietly? You don't have to decide who was right. Just hold both the tears of the one who finally understood and the shock of the one who no longer recognized the room. The bell holds the time.
Jacobson. The layman who built the first Reform-style house of prayer, with an organ, German hymns, and sermons the young could understand. Today's word.
Your line: tears, and people walking out. Today, when you hear someone defend an old way or push a new one, listen for the fear underneath it. Day nine hundred seventy-five.

976.title: Samson Raphael Hirsch
976.hook: Torah joined with worldly life, a founder of modern Orthodoxy
976.howItsDone: Modern Orthodox Jewish schools today commonly teach a dual curriculum of Torah and general studies, and some trace that model to Hirsch's motto, Torah im derekh eretz.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Reform begins: an organ in the synagogue, tears, and people walking out. Your line was tears, and people walking out. Did you hear the fear underneath an argument? Today, a rabbi who answered the same worry another way. Day nine hundred seventy-six.

A schoolboy's bag in Frankfurt. Inside it, a book of the Torah in Hebrew, worn at the corners. Next to it, a German grammar, a geometry book, a history of the ancient world. He'll study all of them today, in the same building, from teachers who keep the Sabbath and the dietary laws without bending them. Nobody in that school thinks the geometry is a threat to the Torah, or the Torah an excuse to skip the geometry. The rabbi who built this school believed both belonged in one bag. His name was Samson Raphael Hirsch.
screen: `ONE SCHOOLBAG.` → `THE TORAH AND A GEOMETRY BOOK.` → `BOTH BELONG IN ONE BAG.`

segments.voice: Hirsch faced the same crisis as the reformers from yesterday: young German Jews drifting from Judaism as they entered German life. But he drew the opposite conclusion about the law. The Torah, he said, was not something to adjust to the times. It was the measure by which the times are judged. So he would not change the service or loosen the commandments. And yet he was no stranger to the modern world. He wrote fine German prose, admired German poets, and wanted Jewish children to learn science, languages and history alongside Torah. His motto came from a line in the Mishnah. In Pirkei Avot, Rabban Gamliel, the son of Rabbi Judah the Prince, says that Torah study is beautiful together with derekh eretz, the way of the land, meaning a worldly occupation, because the effort of both keeps a person from sin. Hirsch took those words, Torah im derekh eretz, Torah with the way of the land, and made them a whole program. For him, derekh eretz meant more than a job. It meant the whole of a cultured, working, civic life, lived inside the commandments rather than beside them. A Jew could be a doctor, a merchant, a reader of poetry and a citizen, and keep every law of the Sabbath while doing it. He built schools in Frankfurt to teach exactly that, and wrote a long commentary on the Torah that is still read. People often name him as a founder of what came to be called modern Orthodoxy. Not every traditional rabbi shared his openness to secular learning, and Orthodox Jews still discuss how far his program reaches. But his answer to the crisis was clear: keep the Torah whole, and bring the world inside it.
screen: `THE TORAH IS THE MEASURE OF THE TIMES.` · `NO CHANGE TO THE LAW.` · `TORAH WITH THE WAY OF THE LAND.` · then, large: `BRING THE WORLD INSIDE IT.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: join Torah and daily work. Sit comfortably and breathe slowly. Think of the ordinary work in front of you today: emails, a shift, the dishes, homework, caring for someone. Now think of one teaching you hold dear, from the Torah or from wherever you draw wisdom. Honesty in business. Rest. Kindness to the stranger. Ask: where in today's work could that teaching live, not beside the work but inside it? One email written more honestly. One task done with care. Just find one place. The bell holds the time.
Hirsch. A Frankfurt rabbi who taught Torah im derekh eretz, Torah joined with worldly life, and is often named a founder of modern Orthodoxy. Today's word.
Your line: torah with the world. Today, take one thing you value into your ordinary work, and let it change how you do one task. Day nine hundred seventy-six.

977.title: Zacharias Frankel
977.hook: a rabbi walks out of a meeting and starts looking for a middle path between tradition and history
977.howItsDone: Conservative Jewish communities study Jewish law alongside its history, and their rabbis make rulings on change through committees that weigh both the tradition and the practice of the community.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Samson Raphael Hirsch, and your line: torah with the world. Did any work of yours feel like it belonged next to the Torah? Today, another German rabbi of the same time, who drew the line in a different place. Day nine hundred seventy-seven.

A room full of rabbis in Frankfurt, in the middle of a long argument. The question on the table sounds small: does Jewish prayer have to be in Hebrew? The meeting leans toward an answer, that Hebrew is welcome but not required. One rabbi, Zacharias Frankel, listens, gathers his papers and leaves. He does not cross over to the other camp either. He spends the rest of his life looking for a road between the two camps in that room. Today, that road.
screen: `A ROOM OF RABBIS IN FRANKFURT.` → `MUST PRAYER BE IN HEBREW?` → `ONE RABBI WALKS OUT.`

segments.voice: By Frankel's day, German Jews were splitting into camps. Reformers, as we heard two days ago, wanted to change prayer and practice to fit modern life. Hirsch, yesterday, held that the law was given whole, and that the work was to live it fully inside the modern world. Frankel heard both, and agreed fully with neither. He was a scholar of history. He read the Mishnah and the Talmud the way a historian reads, asking when a law took shape, and how, and why. He was ready to say that Jewish law had grown and changed over time. That sounded like the reformers. But he drew a different conclusion from it. If the law grew inside the life of the people, then the people's long practice carries real weight. Hebrew in prayer was not just a habit to drop. It was part of the living body of Judaism. So change could come, but slowly, from inside, and with respect for what the people had actually kept. His name for this was positive-historical Judaism. Positive, because the tradition is given and real. Historical, because it has a history and is still moving. He went on to lead a new rabbinical seminary in Breslau, where students learned both the texts and the methods of history. Conservative Judaism, which grew later, looks back on him as a forerunner. Jeremiah has a line that fits his instinct. The prophet tells the people to stand in the ways and look, and to "ask for the old paths, where is the good way, and walk therein." Not to stand frozen where the roads meet, and not to run off in a new direction. To ask the old paths, then walk.
screen: `TWO CAMPS IN GERMANY.` · `LAW WITH A HISTORY.` · `POSITIVE-HISTORICAL JUDAISM.` · then, large: `ASK FOR THE OLD PATHS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: find one middle path. Sit comfortably and let your breath settle. Bring to mind one old habit in your life or your family's, one that someone, maybe you, would like to change. Before deciding anything, ask what it has carried all these years. What has it actually done, over time? Then let one small change appear that keeps what it carried and still moves. You don't have to decide anything now. The bell holds the time.
Zacharias Frankel. The German rabbi and historian who walked out of a debate over Hebrew prayer and taught that Jewish law is both given and growing. Today's word.
Your line: the middle path. Today, before you drop or change one old habit, ask what it has been doing for you. Day nine hundred seventy-seven.

978.title: The Mortara affair (1858)
978.hook: a Jewish boy is taken from his parents in Bologna
978.howItsDone: Jewish historians and teachers retell the Mortara case as part of the story of emancipation, and it is often studied alongside the fight for religious freedom and the rights of parents.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Zacharias Frankel and your line: the middle path. Did you ask what an old habit had been doing for you? Today there is no middle path to find, only a family and a door. Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

Evening, in a house in Bologna. Momolo and Marianna Mortara have put their children to bed. There is a knock. Police of the Papal States are at the door, with an order to take one of the boys, Edgardo. The parents beg. They are given a little time, and then the boy is carried out of the house. His family will spend years trying to bring him back. Today's story is hard, and it is told here plainly.
screen: `A HOUSE IN BOLOGNA.` → `A KNOCK AT NIGHT.` → `EDGARDO IS CARRIED OUT.`

segments.voice: Bologna was then ruled by the pope as a worldly king, and church law was the law of the land. Under that law, a child who had been baptized a Catholic could not be raised by Jewish parents. The family had a Christian servant girl. She said that, years before, when Edgardo was a baby and very sick, she had secretly sprinkled water on him and said the words of baptism, afraid he would die. She told no one at the time. When the story reached church officials, they ruled the boy was now a Catholic, and sent the police. Edgardo was taken to Rome and raised in a house for converts, under the protection of Pope Pius the Ninth himself. His father traveled, wrote, pleaded. Jewish communities in other countries took up the case. Newspapers across Europe and in America printed it, and readers who were not Jewish were troubled too. Governments sent protests. The pope refused to send him home. The ending is harder still. Edgardo grew up inside the Church and became a Catholic priest. He never returned to his parents' faith. When the Papal States later fell, he was old enough to choose, and he chose to stay. The case is remembered by Jews as a wound, and Catholic writers have argued about it in their own way. The Torah has a father's grief like this. When Jacob is told his son Joseph is gone, he tears his clothes and mourns, while the boy is alive and far away, in a foreign land. Genesis gives that grief one short line: "And his father wept for him."
screen: `THE POPE AS A WORLDLY KING.` · `A SECRET BAPTISM.` · `A CASE THE WORLD READ.` · then, large: `AND HIS FATHER WEPT FOR HIM.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: remember a lost child. Sit quietly and let your breathing slow. Bring Edgardo to mind, carried out of his house at night. Then turn to the people left behind: his father traveling and writing, his mother at home, the other children in the next room. Think of anyone you know who is waiting for someone who has not come home. Hold the waiting for a moment, without trying to end it. If you pray, you can remember them in your own words. The bell holds the time.
Mortara. The family name of Edgardo, a Jewish boy in Bologna taken from his parents by the Papal States after a secret baptism was claimed. Today's word.
Your line: the taken child. Today, if you see a parent and child together, let them remind you of the Mortaras at their door. Day nine hundred seventy-eight.

979.title: Yemen
979.hook: an ancient community with its own prayers, melodies and Torah readings
979.howItsDone: In Yemenite synagogues the Torah is read verse by verse with the Aramaic Targum, often chanted by a child, and prayers follow the Tiklal prayer book with melodies handed down in families.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Mortara affair, and your line: the taken child. Did you hold that family in mind for a moment? Today the story turns south and east, away from Europe, to the wider Jewish world. Day nine hundred seventy-nine.

A Shabbat morning in a Yemenite synagogue. The Torah scroll is open. A reader chants a verse in Hebrew, in a melody of its own, rising and falling. Then he stops, and a young boy beside him chants the same verse again, this time in Aramaic. Verse by verse, Hebrew, then Aramaic, back and forth, all the way through the reading. Nobody is rushing, not the reader and not the boy. Today, the Jews of Yemen.
screen: `A SHABBAT MORNING.` → `A VERSE IN HEBREW.` → `THE SAME VERSE IN ARAMAIC.`

segments.voice: Yemen sits at the bottom corner of the Arabian peninsula. Jews lived there for a very long time, and tradition tells of their arrival in the days of the Bible. Far from the big centers of Jewish learning, they kept their own ways. First, the reading. That Aramaic voice is the Targum, an ancient translation of the Torah. In many places it stopped being read aloud in the synagogue. Yemenite Jews kept the custom, and in their congregations a child often reads the Targum, so the young learn by doing. Second, the prayers. Yemenite Jews have their own prayer book, called the Tiklal, with its own order and its own melodies. Prayer and song were passed down mostly by ear, in families, in the same small synagogues. Third, the poetry. A beloved Yemenite poet, Shalom Shabazi, wrote songs that are still sung at weddings and Shabbat tables, mixing Hebrew, Aramaic and Arabic. When the State of Israel was new, Jews from Yemen were flown there in an airlift people named after a verse from Exodus. There God tells Israel: "I bore you on eagles' wings, and brought you unto Myself." People who had never seen an airplane, tradition says, recognized it from that verse. In Israel the melodies came along, and singers from Yemenite families carried them into new music. And in Yemenite synagogues in Israel, a child may still stand beside the reader, ready with the Aramaic.
screen: `A CORNER OF ARABIA.` · `THE TARGUM READ ALOUD.` · `THE TIKLAL AND SHABAZI'S SONGS.` · then, large: `ON EAGLES' WINGS.`

segments.voice: Here's today's practice: learn one Yemenite custom. Sit still and let your breath slow. Bring back the picture of the synagogue: the Hebrew verse, then the boy's voice with the same verse in Aramaic. Let your breathing follow that pattern, one breath to hear, one breath to repeat. Then think of one thing in your own life you learned by repeating after someone older. Who taught it to you? Hold them in mind. The bell holds the time.
Yemen. Home to a Jewish community that kept the Targum read aloud, its own prayer book, the Tiklal, and the songs of Shalom Shabazi. Today's word.
Your line: a child reads the Targum. Today, look up one recording of a Yemenite Jewish melody, and listen to it once all the way through. Day nine hundred seventy-nine.

980.title: Morocco
980.hook: the night Passover ends, Moroccan Jewish homes open their doors to neighbors for Mimouna
980.howItsDone: On the night Passover ends, Moroccan Jewish families set a table with mufleta pancakes, honey, milk and greenery, visit from house to house with blessings, and in Israel the next day often brings large outdoor picnics.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Yemen: the Targum read verse by verse, and your line, a child reads the Targum. Did you find a melody to listen to? Today, across North Africa to Morocco, and the last day of this week. Day nine hundred eighty.

Passover ends at nightfall. For a week, no bread in the house. And in Moroccan Jewish homes, almost as the last blessing is said, the kitchen comes alive. Flour comes out. Thin pancakes go into the pan, to be eaten warm with butter and honey. The table fills with sweets, fresh milk, green stalks of wheat. The front door stays open, and the neighbors come in, Jewish and not. Today's word is the name of that night.
screen: `PASSOVER ENDS AT NIGHTFALL.` → `PANCAKES WITH BUTTER AND HONEY.` → `THE DOOR STAYS OPEN.`

segments.voice: Mimouna. Nobody is quite sure where the name comes from. Some connect it to Maimon, the father of Maimonides, said to have died around this time of year. Others hear in it the Hebrew emunah, faith, or an Arabic word for good fortune. The custom is clearer than the name. On Mimouna night, families set a table that looks like a wish for the year ahead: honey for sweetness, milk for plenty, wheat for a good harvest, sometimes a fish for blessing. Guests walk from house to house, and people greet each other with a Judeo-Arabic blessing for success and good luck. Then there are the neighbors. In Morocco, tradition says, Muslim neighbors would bring flour, butter and milk to Jewish homes as Passover ended, since their own kitchens had none, and stay to eat. The party became a meeting place. When Moroccan Jews moved to Israel, they brought Mimouna with them, and the open door became an open park, with picnics that welcome whoever comes. The Torah gives a simple rule that this night acts out: "thou shalt love thy neighbour as thyself." Mimouna turns that into flour, pancakes and an unlocked door. Look back at this week, too. A Sanhedrin called by Napoleon. Reform beginning. Hirsch joining Torah with the world. Frankel's middle path. The Mortaras' terrible night. The Targum in Yemen. And now a door in Morocco, wide open after Passover.
